Let $f(x)=y={x}^{4}-{x}^{2}$ and $g(x)={x}^{3}-x.$ First, we find the intersections of the two curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =g(x) \\ {x}^{4}-{x}^{2} & ={x}^{3}-x \\ {x}^{2}({x}^{2}-1) & =x({x}^{2}-1) \\ ({x}^{2}-x)({x}^{2}-1) & =0 \\ ({x}^{2}-x)(x+1)(x-1) & =0 \\ x(x-1)(x+1)(x-1) & =0 \\ x & =-1,0,1\end{aligned}
$$

The area we want consists of two regions: ${A}_{1}$ and ${A}_{2}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14220560/assets/d84bd9bccba15a91ab54ee0dc64fb344c191384a14ee5d5c2fb857dc18fc63db.png)

We have:

- For the area ${A}_{1},$ we have $x\in [-1,0],$ and the upper function is $g(x)$ while the lower function is $f(x).$ So, the area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}[g(x)-f(x)]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}[({x}^{3}-x)-({x}^{4}-{x}^{2})]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(-{x}^{4}+{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}-x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the area ${A}_{2},$ we have $x\in [0,1],$ and the upper function is $f(x)$ while the lower function is $g(x).$ So, the area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[f(x)-g(x)]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[({x}^{4}-{x}^{2})-({x}^{3}-x)]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{4}-{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the required area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={A}_{1}+{A}_{2} \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(-{x}^{4}+{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}-x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{4}-{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

  • For the area A2, we have x∈[0,1], and the upper function is f(x) while the lower function is g(x). So, the area is given by A2=∫01[f(x)−g(x)]dx=∫01[(x4−x2)−(x3−x)]dx=∫01(x4−x3−x2+x)dx.
